why_how.text: Slow vehicles change the math of the road, so drivers must judge closing speed early and stay patient.
Funeral processions move as one group, so the law lets them stay together and limits how others may interact with them.

scenario.text: Riley is driving on a two-lane road behind a funeral procession heading the same way.

reasoning.text: A driver going the same way as a procession must not pass it unless the road has two or more lanes in the procession's direction.

result.text: Riley stays behind the procession until it turns off or the road widens to two lanes in that direction.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a same-direction driver may pass a funeral procession whenever it is moving slowly.

correction.text: Oncoming drivers may choose to yield, but same-direction drivers are forbidden to pass unless there are two or more lanes in its direction.

memory_support.text: Only with two lanes its way.

prompt.text: Riley is behind a funeral procession on a two-lane road going the same way. May Riley pass?

answer.text: No. Passing is allowed only with two or more lanes in the procession's direction.

rationale.text: Oncoming drivers may choose to yield, but same-direction drivers must not pass on a road like this.

narration.text: This chapter is about how you move: your lane, your speed, curves, turns and following distance. It starts with two kinds of slow-moving traffic. First, farm equipment, which is allowed on most North Carolina roads and which drivers often approach far too quickly. Second, funeral processions, which have special rights to stay together through intersections, and which other drivers must treat with care. You will learn the procession's lighting and spacing, when it may go through an intersection, and the very different rules for oncoming drivers and for drivers going the same direction.

lines.text: The gap closes faster than expected.

narration.text: Because farm equipment moves so slowly, the gap closes much faster than you expect as you come up behind it. A tractor that looks far away at the top of a hill can be right in front of you a few seconds later. So slow down as soon as you spot farm equipment, rather than waiting until you are close. Farm equipment is allowed by law on most North Carolina roads, but not on interstates. That means you will meet it on two-lane rural roads and highways, where passing room is limited and patience is the safest choice. Respect the gap.

lines.text: Follow as closely as is prudent.

narration.text: Every vehicle in a funeral procession must drive with headlights on, and with hazard flashers on as well if it has them. Those lights mark the procession clearly for everyone else on the road. Procession vehicles keep to the right side of the road and follow the car ahead as closely as is reasonable and prudent, so no gaps open up for outside traffic to slip into. If you are part of a procession, stay alert and leave enough room to stop, but keep the line tight. If you are outside it, the lights tell you which cars belong together.

lines.text: The lead car obeys all signals.
Others may follow through with care.

narration.text: The lead vehicle of a procession obeys all traffic signals. But once it has crossed an intersection lawfully, or when an officer or funeral director directs it, or a police vehicle leads, the rest of the procession may go through the intersection without stopping, using extra care. That can mean procession cars going through a red light. If you are an outside driver, never knowingly drive between vehicles in a procession, and when it goes through a red light, do not enter the intersection on your green unless you can do so safely without crossing its path.

title.text: Through for them, wait for you

lines.text: Procession cars may follow the lead through.
Outside drivers on green must not cut across.

narration.text: Here is the trap. An outside driver who sees a green light may think it is safe to go, even while procession cars are still passing through on red. It is not. Procession cars may continue through an intersection behind a lead car that crossed lawfully, while an outside driver facing green must not cut across the procession's path. Practice questions often ask whether the green light gives the outside driver priority. It does not, if entering would cross the procession. Wait until the last procession car has cleared, then proceed when it is safe.

lines.text: Oncoming drivers may choose to yield.
If so, slow or stop off the road.
Same direction: no passing without two lanes.

narration.text: An oncoming driver may choose to yield to a procession, as a mark of respect. If they do, they must either slow down or stop fully off the roadway, so other oncoming traffic can stay in its lane. Stopping in the travel lane is not allowed. A driver going the same way as a procession has a stricter rule. That driver must not pass the procession, unless the road is marked with two or more lanes moving in the procession's direction. So on a two-lane road, a driver behind a procession simply follows until the procession turns off.

Here is a quick check: Riley is driving on a two-lane road and comes up behind a funeral procession heading the same way. The procession is moving slowly, and the oncoming lane looks clear. May Riley pass? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. A driver going the same way as a procession must not pass it unless the road is marked with two or more lanes moving in the procession's direction. Oncoming drivers may choose to yield, but same-direction drivers on a road like this simply follow until the procession turns off.

lines.text: Same direction: no passing without two lanes.

narration.text: Let us recap. You close on farm equipment much faster than you expect, so slow early, and remember it is allowed on most roads but not interstates. Every procession vehicle uses headlights, and flashers if it has them, keeps right and follows closely. Procession cars may go through an intersection behind a lead car that crossed lawfully or when directed, while outside drivers must not cut across its path, even on green. Oncoming drivers may choose to yield by slowing or stopping off the road, and same-direction drivers must not pass unless there are two or more lanes in its direction.

why_how.text: Keeping right keeps traffic predictable, so faster traffic can pass on the left and oncoming traffic has its space.
Stopping distance grows quickly with speed, so faster driving needs more space and a longer view ahead.

scenario.text: Pat is driving below the posted limit in the left lane of a three-lane highway.

reasoning.text: On a multi-lane highway, a driver going slower than the posted limit should use the far right lane except when passing, turning left or avoiding an obstruction.

result.text: Pat signals and moves to the far right lane, letting faster traffic pass on the left.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a slower driver may cruise in any lane on a multi-lane highway.

correction.text: Slower traffic belongs in the far right lane, and driving on the left is lawful only in cases like one-way streets and passing.

prompt.text: Pat is cruising below the limit in the left lane of a three-lane highway with no turn coming up. Which lane should Pat use?

rationale.text: Slower traffic uses the far right lane except when passing, turning left or avoiding an obstruction.

narration.text: This lesson covers two basics that shape almost every trip: which part of the road you use, and how speed affects your ability to stop. You will learn the law about driving on the right side of the road, the lane slower drivers should use on multi-lane highways, how speed and reaction time together set your stopping distance, how far a car needs to stop at fifty-five miles per hour, how each extra mile per hour costs control, and why higher speed means you must look farther ahead. These ideas set up the speed limit rules in the next lessons.

lines.text: The law requires the right side.
Left only for one-way streets and passing.

narration.text: The law requires driving on the right side of the road. The left side is legal only in cases such as one-way streets and passing. On a multi-lane highway, if you are going slower than the posted limit, use the far right lane, except when passing, turning left or avoiding an obstruction. This keeps traffic predictable. Faster drivers pass on the left, slower drivers keep right, and nobody has to weave around a slow car sitting in a passing lane. If you find yourself in the left lane with traffic stacking up behind you, signal and move right when it is safe.

lines.text: Left side: one-way streets and passing.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers treat every lane of a highway as equal, or think the left side of a two-lane road is fine whenever no one is coming. Neither is right. Driving on the left is lawful only in situations such as one-way streets and passing, while slower traffic on a multi-lane highway belongs in the far right lane. On practice questions, an option that lets a slow driver cruise in the left lane, or that allows driving on the left side for convenience, is the wrong one. The right side is the rule, and the left is the exception.

lines.text: About two hundred eleven feet at fifty-five.

narration.text: Your speed and your reaction time together set your stopping distance. First, there is the distance you travel while you notice a hazard and move your foot to the brake. Then there is the braking distance itself. Higher speed lengthens both. Even in ideal conditions, a vehicle going fifty-five miles per hour needs about two hundred eleven feet to come to a complete stop. That is roughly two-thirds of a football field, on a dry road with an alert driver. In rain, at night, or with a distracted or tired driver, the real distance is longer.

lines.text: Each extra mile per hour costs control.

narration.text: Every extra mile per hour reduces your control of the vehicle, and higher speed raises the chance that a crash will cause serious injury or death. So speed is not only about getting there sooner. It changes how well you can steer and stop, and how badly people are hurt when something goes wrong. Because stopping takes more room at higher speed, the faster you travel, the farther ahead you need to see so that you have room to stop. On a fast road, scan well down the road, not just at the car in front of you. Scan well ahead.

lines.text: Below the limit in the left lane.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Pat is driving a little below the posted limit in the left lane of a three-lane highway. Pat is not passing anyone and has no left turn coming up, and faster cars keep stacking up behind. Which lane should Pat use? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the far right lane. On a multi-lane highway, a driver going slower than the posted limit should use the far right lane except when passing, turning left or avoiding an obstruction. Pat should signal, check mirrors and blind spot, and move right.

lines.text: Drive right; left only by exception.
Faster means farther to stop and see.

narration.text: To wrap up, the law requires driving on the right side of the road, with the left side lawful only in cases such as one-way streets and passing. On multi-lane highways, slower drivers use the far right lane except when passing, turning left or avoiding an obstruction. Speed and reaction time together set stopping distance, and even in ideal conditions a car at fifty-five miles per hour needs about two hundred eleven feet to stop. Every extra mile per hour costs control and raises injury risk, and the faster you go, the farther ahead you need to see.

why_how.text: Crashes happen when speeds differ sharply, so driving far below the flow is risky as well as speeding.
The safe speed is the one that fits the conditions, never above the posted limit.

scenario.text: Casey is nervous on a busy highway and drives far below the limit, and a long line of cars builds up behind.

reasoning.text: Driving well below the limit is dangerous, slow drivers must keep any posted minimum, and a line of traffic should be let past.

result.text: Casey pulls to the side at a safe spot, lets the vehicles go by, then rejoins at a steady safe speed.

claim.text: Many people think driving as slowly as possible is always the safest choice.

correction.text: Driving well under the limit is also linked to more crashes, so the goal is a speed suited to conditions within the posted range.

prompt.text: Casey drives far below the limit on a busy highway, with a long line of cars behind. What should Casey do?

answer.text: Pull to the side at a safe spot and let the vehicles go by.

rationale.text: Very slow driving is dangerous, and letting the line pass reduces the risk to everyone.

narration.text: Most speed lessons focus on going too fast, and that matters. But this handbook is just as clear that going too slowly is dangerous. This lesson covers both ends. You will learn why driving well below the limit raises risk, where slow driving is most dangerous, what to do when traffic stacks up behind you, what studies say about slow drivers, and the two upper limits your speed must never cross. The goal is not the slowest speed or the fastest, but a speed that fits the road, the traffic and the conditions, within the posted range.

lines.text: Driving well below the limit is dangerous.
Studies link slow drivers to crashes.

narration.text: Driving well below the limit is also dangerous. If you must go slowly, you still have to keep to any posted minimum speed. The handbook cites studies finding that a vehicle going well under the posted limit is far more likely to cause or be in a crash than one moving at normal speed. The reason is speed difference. When one car moves much slower than the traffic around it, other drivers have to brake hard, change lanes suddenly or pass in risky places. A big speed gap between vehicles creates conflict, whichever direction the gap runs.

title.text: Hills, curves and lines of cars

lines.text: Very slow over a hilltop is risky.
Very slow around a curve is risky.
Let a line of traffic pass.

narration.text: Very slow driving is especially risky just over the top of a hill or around a curve, where faster traffic may hit you before it can slow down. A driver coming over a crest at normal speed has little time to react to a slow car just beyond it. If you have to drive slowly, choose roads and times where you can be seen well ahead. And if a line of traffic builds behind you, it is wise to pull to the side, stop and let the vehicles go by. That removes the pressure on you and the temptation for others to pass unsafely. Visibility matters.

Here is the trap. Many learners assume that the slowest possible speed is always the safest. The handbook disagrees. Speeding reduces control and raises injury risk, yet driving well under the limit is also linked to more crashes, so the goal is a speed suited to conditions within the posted range. On practice questions, beware of options that praise driving as slowly as possible, or that treat the posted limit as a target in every condition. The right answer usually describes a speed that fits the traffic, the weather and the road, without going over the limit.

lines.text: Never above a safe speed for conditions.

narration.text: There are two upper limits on your speed. Never go faster than the posted limit, and never go faster than is reasonable and wise for the conditions at the time. Rain, fog, darkness, heavy traffic, construction or a narrow road can each make the safe speed lower than the posted one. So safe driving often means going slower than the posted limit, but never faster. The posted limit is the maximum for good conditions, not a promise that the speed is safe right now. When conditions get worse, your speed should come down with them.

lines.text: Far below the limit on a busy highway.
A long line of cars behind.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Casey feels nervous on a busy highway and drives far below the posted limit. A long line of cars has built up behind, and some drivers are starting to pass in risky places. What should Casey do? Work it out before reading on. Casey should pull to the side at a safe spot, stop and let the vehicles go by. Driving well below the limit is dangerous, slow drivers must still keep to any posted minimum, and the handbook advises letting a line of traffic pass. Then Casey can rejoin at a steady, safe speed.

lines.text: Let a line of traffic pass.

narration.text: Let us recap. Driving well below the limit is dangerous, and slow drivers must keep any posted minimum. It is especially risky just over a hill or around a curve, and studies cited in the handbook link slow vehicles to far more crashes. If a line of traffic builds behind you, pull to the side and let it pass. At the other end, never go faster than the posted limit or faster than is reasonable for conditions. Safe driving often means slower than the limit, but never faster. The goal is a speed suited to conditions within the posted range.

why_how.text: Default limits protect people where signs are missing, so drivers must know them by heart.
Buses carrying students have their own maximums, set below or equal to the road limits.

scenario.text: Jordan drives a school activity bus from town to a game on a rural highway with no posted limit signs.

reasoning.text: The maximum is fifty-five miles per hour for school activity buses and fifty-five outside cities and towns.

result.text: Jordan keeps the activity bus at or below fifty-five, and would keep a regular school bus at or below forty-five.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a school activity bus has the same forty-five miles per hour limit as a regular school bus.

correction.text: A regular school bus is held to forty-five, while a school activity bus may go up to fifty-five, the same as the rural limit.

prompt.text: Jordan drives a school activity bus on a rural highway with no signs. What is the maximum speed?

rationale.text: Activity buses share the fifty-five figure with rural roads, while regular school buses are held to forty-five.

lines.text: Default limits where signs are missing.

narration.text: This lesson is short but packed with numbers that practice questions love. You will learn the default speed limit in cities and towns when no sign says otherwise, the maximum speeds outside cities and towns and on interstates, and the separate maximums for school buses and school activity buses. Two of these limits share the same figure, which is exactly the kind of detail that shows up as a trick question. As you go, connect each number to the place or vehicle it belongs to, rather than memorizing a bare list of numbers.

lines.text: Cities and towns: thirty-five unless posted.

narration.text: Unless a sign says otherwise, the speed limit in cities and towns is thirty-five miles per hour. Outside cities and towns, the maximum speed is fifty-five miles per hour, and on interstates it is seventy miles per hour. Posted signs can set different limits, and you must follow them. But when no sign is posted, these defaults apply. So entering a town without a speed sign means thirty-five, leaving town onto a rural highway means up to fifty-five, and an interstate allows up to seventy, always subject to the rule of never driving faster than conditions allow.

Here is a numbers trap. The default limit inside cities and towns is thirty-five miles per hour unless posted otherwise, while interstates allow up to seventy miles per hour. Practice questions often offer forty-five or fifty-five as the city default, borrowing numbers from other rules. Forty-five belongs to regular school buses, and fifty-five belongs to roads outside towns and to activity buses. Keep each number tied to its place. Thirty-five is the town default when no sign is posted. Seventy is the interstate maximum. Neither is a number for buses.

Buses carrying students have their own maximums. The maximum speed is forty-five miles per hour for school buses and fifty-five miles per hour for school activity buses. A school activity bus carries students to events such as games and field trips. So a regular school bus is the slowest vehicle on this list, even on a road where cars may go fifty-five or seventy. As a driver sharing the road, expect school buses to move at or below forty-five, and plan your following distance and any legal pass with that slower speed in mind.

Here is a quick check: Jordan drives a school activity bus from town to an away game, traveling on a rural highway with no posted speed limit signs. What is the maximum speed Jordan may drive? Work it out before reading on. The answer is fifty-five miles per hour. The maximum for a school activity bus is fifty-five, which also matches the maximum outside cities and towns. If Jordan were driving a regular school bus instead, the maximum would be forty-five miles per hour, no matter what the road limit was. Know the bus type.

lines.text: Towns thirty-five, rural fifty-five, interstate seventy.

narration.text: To finish, unless a sign says otherwise, the speed limit in cities and towns is thirty-five miles per hour. The maximum is fifty-five miles per hour outside cities and towns and seventy miles per hour on interstates. School buses may go no faster than forty-five miles per hour, and school activity buses no faster than fifty-five. That fifty-five figure is shared by the rural limit and the activity bus maximum, while the regular school bus is held to forty-five. And remember, these are maximums, never targets when conditions call for less.

why_how.text: Braking in a curve can break traction, so speed is set before the curve and gently increased through it.
Gravity pushes a car faster downhill, so downhill curves need a lower gear and earlier braking.

scenario.text: Taylor approaches a sharp downhill curve on a mountain road.

reasoning.text: Taylor should allow for gravity, shift to a lower gear before the descent, and brake earlier and slower than on level ground.

result.text: Taylor gears down at the top, slows before the bend, steers just before it, and eases speed up through the curve.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should brake firmly in the middle of a curve to control speed.

correction.text: The speed reduction happens before the curve, and speed is then gradually increased through it rather than reduced by braking inside it.

prompt.text: Taylor is about to start down a steep hill that ends in a curve. When should Taylor shift down and start braking?

answer.text: Before the descent, braking earlier and slower than on flat road.

rationale.text: On a downhill curve, the lower gear and early braking come before the descent, not once in the bend.

narration.text: Curves are where speed and traction meet. A car that enters a curve too fast can slide off the road, and braking hard in the middle of the curve can make it worse. This lesson walks through the handbook's method for curves: slowing down before you enter, gently adding speed through the curve, braking gradually if you have no choice, starting to steer at the right moment and keeping right, and handling the extra challenge of a downhill curve, where gravity is working against you. Practice questions focus on the order of these steps.

lines.text: No braking needed in the curve.

narration.text: For a curve, slow down before you enter, so you do not need to brake in it. Then gradually add speed through the curve to keep traction and control. That gentle acceleration settles the car's weight and helps the tires grip. Start steering just before the point where the road begins to bend, and stay on your own side, as far right as you can. Drifting toward the center line in a curve puts you in the path of oncoming traffic that may also be cutting the corner. So the pattern is slow, steer, then ease the speed back up as the road straightens.

title.text: Brake before, not in, the bend

lines.text: Speed comes off before the curve.
Then speed builds gently through it.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers enter a curve at full speed and then brake once they feel the car leaning. That is backwards. On a curve, the speed reduction happens before the curve, and speed is then gradually increased through it rather than reduced by braking inside it. Braking in the curve shifts weight forward and can break the tires' grip just when you need it most. On practice questions, choose the answer that slows the car before the curve. Reject any answer that has you braking hard in the middle. Memory line: slow before, ease through.

lines.text: Build to steady pressure only when safe.

narration.text: Sometimes something unexpected happens in a curve, and braking cannot be avoided. In that case, press the brakes gradually until you are sure that steady pressure is safe. Sudden, hard braking in a curve can lock the wheels or cause a skid, sending the car straight instead of around the bend. Gradual braking lets you slow while keeping the tires gripping the road. This is the fallback, not the plan. The plan is still to slow down before the curve, so that braking inside it is something you rarely need to do at all.

lines.text: Shift to a lower gear before the descent.

narration.text: A downhill curve adds gravity to the problem. The car naturally picks up speed going down, so you need more distance to slow down. For a downhill curve, allow for gravity, shift to a lower gear before the descent, and brake earlier and slower than you would on level ground. The lower gear lets the engine help hold the car back, so the brakes do not have to do all the work. Doing this before the descent matters, because shifting or braking hard once you are already in the bend can upset the car's balance and grip. Plan the descent.

Here is a quick check: Taylor is driving on a mountain road and is about to start down a steep hill that ends in a sharp curve. When should Taylor shift down and start braking? Work it out before reading on. The answer is before the descent, braking earlier and slower than on flat road. On a downhill curve, you allow for gravity by shifting to a lower gear before going down and braking early, not once you are already in the bend. Then Taylor steers just before the curve begins and eases speed up gently through it. Gear first, then brakes.

lines.text: Downhill: gear down and brake early.

narration.text: To wrap up, slow down before entering a curve so you need not brake in it, then gradually add speed through it to keep traction and control. If braking in a curve cannot be avoided, press the brakes gradually until steady pressure is safe. Start steering just before the road begins to bend, and stay on your side as far right as you can. For a downhill curve, allow for gravity, shift to a lower gear before the descent, and brake earlier and slower than on level ground, never waiting until you are in the bend. Slow first, then steer.

why_how.text: Following too closely is a leading cause of crashes, so a measured gap gives you time to react.
Lane changes and turns put you across other drivers' paths, so careful checks prevent side and blind-spot crashes.

scenario.text: Lee wants to move one lane left on a four-lane highway, and another car is two lanes over.

reasoning.text: On a multi-lane highway, check both the lane you are moving into and the lane beyond it, in case another driver is heading for the same space.

result.text: Lee checks mirrors, looks over a shoulder, sees the far car signaling toward the same lane, and waits.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a lane change only needs a check of the lane you are moving into.

correction.text: On a multi-lane road you also check the lane beyond your target, because a driver there may be moving into the same space.

prompt.text: Lee is about to move one lane left on a four-lane highway. Besides the target lane, what else should Lee check?

answer.text: The lane beyond the target lane.

rationale.text: A driver in the lane beyond may be heading for the same space, so both lanes need checking.

narration.text: This final lesson in the chapter is about the space around your car. You will learn how to position your car for a right turn, why motorcycles and bicycles need extra attention when you turn, how much following distance to leave and how to measure it with the two-second rule, and how to change lanes safely, including a check that many drivers skip on multi-lane highways. Each of these habits protects the space in front of you, beside you or behind you, and together they prevent many of the most common crash types on busy roads.

lines.text: Stay close to the right edge.
Slow before, then speed up slightly.

narration.text: On a right turn, keep close to the right edge so no vehicle can squeeze in between you and the curb. Slow before turning, and then speed up slightly as you complete the turn. Before any turn, remember that motorcycles and bicycles are particularly hard to see while you turn, so always signal and look before turning. A bicycle in a bike lane or a motorcycle partly hidden by another car can be right where you plan to go. A clear signal warns them, and a careful look catches them before the turn begins rather than halfway through it.

lines.text: Leave room for a passer to move in.
Two seconds behind a fixed point.

narration.text: Following too closely is a leading cause of crashes. On the open road, leave enough space ahead that a passing vehicle could safely move into it. To measure that space, use the two-second rule. Watch the vehicle ahead pass a fixed point, such as a sign or a tree. Then count the time until you reach that point. If it is less than two seconds, you are too close, so ease off. Two seconds gives you time to notice the car ahead braking and to brake yourself. In rain or at higher speed, allow more than two seconds. More is better.

lines.text: Two-second rule: gap to the car ahead.
Higher speed: look farther down the road.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two ideas about distance are easy to blend. The two-second rule governs the gap to the car ahead, while seeing farther ahead is what you need as speed rises, because stopping distance grows. One is about how far behind the next car you stay. The other is about how far down the road your eyes scan. Practice questions sometimes describe the two-second rule as looking two seconds ahead, or claim sight distance can shrink at high speed. Both are wrong. Keep the gap at two seconds or more, and look farther ahead as you go faster.

To change lanes, check the side and rear-view mirrors, look over your shoulder to clear the blind spot, signal ahead of time, and then move over. The shoulder check matters because mirrors leave a blind spot beside and slightly behind your car, large enough to hide another vehicle. On a highway with several lanes, check both the lane you are moving into and the lane beyond it, in case another driver is heading for the same space. Two cars moving into the same lane from opposite sides at the same moment is a common, avoidable crash.

lines.text: Check the lane beyond it too.

narration.text: Here is the second trap. Many drivers check only the lane they want to move into. On a multi-lane road, that is not enough. A lane change on a multi-lane road needs a check of the lane beyond your target lane too, because a driver there may be moving into the same space. Picture a three-lane highway. You move from the right lane to the center, and at the same moment a driver in the left lane moves to the center as well. Checking that far lane, and watching for its signals, prevents that collision. Memory line: check the lane beyond.

Here is a quick check: Lee is driving on a four-lane highway and wants to move one lane to the left. Lee has checked the mirrors and looked over a shoulder at the lane next door, which is empty. What else should Lee check before moving? Work it out before reading on. Lee should also check the lane beyond the target lane. On a multi-lane highway, a driver in that far lane may be heading for the same space at the same moment. If that driver is signaling toward the center, Lee waits, then signals and moves when it is clear.

lines.text: Hug the right edge; look for bikes.

narration.text: To finish the chapter, on a right turn keep close to the right edge, slow before the turn and speed up slightly after, and always signal and look for motorcycles and bicycles before turning. Following too closely is a leading cause of crashes, so leave room for a passing vehicle to move in, and use the two-second rule to measure your gap, while looking farther ahead as speed rises. To change lanes, check mirrors, look over your shoulder, signal ahead of time and then move, and on multi-lane roads check the lane beyond your target lane too.
